lesson.title: Reading and Writing Limit Notation Fluently
lesson.summary: Limit notation packs a function, a target value, and a resulting number into one compact expression, and reading it fluently now pays off immediately once derivative and integral notation build directly on top of it.
lesson.body:
Once you understand what a limit means, the next skill is reading and writing the notation quickly and correctly, because limit notation shows up in nearly every calculus formula from here forward. The expression lim(x to a) f(x) = L is read aloud as "the limit of f(x) as x approaches a equals L." Each symbol carries specific information: "lim" announces that a limiting process is happening, the notation x to a names both the input variable (x) and the target value it is heading toward (a), and the equation "= L" states the resulting output value, if one exists.

It helps to separate the three pieces mentally. The function, f(x), is the rule being evaluated. The target, a, is a fixed real number on the number line that x is approaching, though a does not have to be in the domain of f. The limit value, L, is also a fixed real number, the number the outputs settle near; it is a completely different quantity from f(a), even when both happen to exist and to be equal.

Take the straightforward example lim(x to 3) (2x + 1) = 7. Reading it aloud: "the limit of 2x plus 1, as x approaches 3, equals 7." Here the function is f(x) = 2x + 1, the target is a = 3, and the claimed limit value is L = 7. Because this function is a simple polynomial with no division or other troublesome operation, direct substitution actually works: f(3) = 2(3) + 1 = 7, so the limit and the function value agree in this case. Checking with nearby inputs: f(2.9) = 6.8, f(3.1) = 7.2, f(2.99) = 6.98, f(3.01) = 7.02. All of these outputs are converging on 7 as the inputs converge on 3, confirming the notation's claim.

The letter used for the input variable is never special. lim(t to 5) (t^2 + 1) means exactly the same kind of statement as lim(x to 5) (x^2 + 1); only the label changes, not the meaning, since t and x are both just placeholders for "the input." It is also worth stressing what the notation deliberately leaves out: it never mentions f(a) directly, because, as the previous section showed with (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1), the limit can exist and be perfectly well defined even when f(a) itself is undefined.

Two notational cousins will appear soon: lim(x to a-) f(x), read "the limit as x approaches a from the left," and lim(x to a+) f(x), read "from the right," each restricting which side of a the input is allowed to approach from. The plain lim(x to a) f(x), with no plus or minus mark, always means both sides at once, approaching a with no restriction on direction.

Getting fluent with this notation now pays off immediately, because derivative and integral notation are both built directly on top of limit notation, using exactly the same lim(x to a) syntax with the target and the expression changed. Misreading a subscript or dropping the arrow is a common early mistake, so it is worth practicing saying each limit expression out loud in full words until the symbols stop feeling foreign.
